sources.title: Air Stones: The Secret Weapon Every Aquarium Needs to Have – Aquarium Co-Op
Máy Sủi Oxy Cho Bể Cá Cảnh: Hướng Dẫn Toàn Diện Từ A Đến Z Để Cá Khỏe Mạnh

facts.fact: Aeration means adding air to the tank with an air pump, airline tubing and an air outlet such as an air stone, sponge filter or moving bed filter.
Gas exchange happens at the water surface: carbon dioxide leaves the water and oxygen from the air dissolves in, and good surface agitation is the key to it.
Turbulent surface flow gives the best gas exchange, while smooth (laminar) flow gives only slight aeration.
A smooth water surface gives about 5% of the aeration of a choppy surface of the same size.
Rising bubbles aerate by creating turbulent flow at the surface.
Ideal dissolved oxygen in a freshwater tank is about 7 to 8 ppm (mg/L), which can be measured with a test kit or digital meter.
Fully saturated water at 78°F holds 8.25 ppm (mg/L) of oxygen, and warm water holds less oxygen than cold water.
A dissolved oxygen level of 5 mg/L or more is recommended for optimum fish health, and most fish species are distressed when it falls to 2–4 mg/L.

The air pump pushes air through the air stone to make fine bubbles that help oxygen dissolve in the water; too little dissolved oxygen can suffocate fish, especially in crowded or warm tanks or when fish are sick.
Name for the term: "máy sục khí"
Name for the term: "máy sủi oxy"
Name for the term: "đá sủi khí (air stone)"
Signs of low oxygen include fish resting on the bottom, low appetite, rapid gill movement and gasping at the surface.
Signs of poor aeration include fish hanging at the surface, piping and rapid gill movement in still water; in strong current, fish swim with gaping mouths.
Dying fish may gasp for oxygen at the surface, which is called "piping".
Common causes of low oxygen are high water temperature, too many fish, certain medications or chemical treatments, and too little surface agitation.
In a test, floating plants covering the surface of a 55-gallon tank gave significantly lower oxygen.
In an oxygen emergency, a large water change adds oxygen immediately.
If fish are dying from low dissolved oxygen, the most important step is to turn on an aerator.
Put the air pump in a dry place above the water line so water cannot flow back into it when the power is off.
If the pump must sit below the water line, fit a check valve ("van một chiều (check valve)") on the airline to protect it.
A check valve stops water flowing back into the airline tubing and the pump.
Replace the air stone when its bubbles become uneven or it clogs.
An airstone aerates well only if the pump is big enough to produce hundreds of bubbles per second; small pumps sold in kits or stores give little aeration.
Filter outlets, wavemakers and powerheads that make a choppy surface give excellent aeration.
In a test, a powerhead aimed at the surface did better than a venturi powerhead, and a circulation pump did not significantly raise oxygen.
In a test, a 40-gallon breeder tank with a sponge filter had higher oxygen than a 55-gallon tank because it had more surface area.
Strong aeration drives CO2 down to roughly 2–3 ppm, while plants do best above 10 ppm CO2, so aeration works against planted tanks that use added CO2.
Low-tech tanks with few fish may skip aeration, but moderately stocked tanks need it.
In dry climates, air pumps and airstones can increase evaporation, so choppy surface waves are preferred there.
Letting floating plants cover the whole surface limits gas exchange.
Placing the air pump below the water line without a check valve lets water flow back into it.
The air pump draws room air into the tank, so aerosols, floor-stripping chemicals and insect sprays can kill fish; scents are not a problem.
Remove fish before a house is tented for fumigation, because the gas gets into tanks even when they are covered with plastic wrap or foil and the pumps are off.

Thủy Sinh 24H, a Vietnamese shop, sells battery backup air pumps ("Máy dùng pin (dự phòng)") that switch on automatically when the mains power fails; the shop calls them essential where power cuts are frequent, but they run only for a short time.
Aquarium Science calls the rule of '12 square inches of surface per inch of fish' a myth.
Aquarium Science says a 2-inch fish needs eight times the aeration of a 1-inch fish, not twice as much.
Aquarium Science says the ratio of surface area to depth is meaningless for judging aeration.
Aquarium Science says diffusion alone is not enough for moderately or heavily stocked tanks.
